answer_text:
Switching to the metric system in the United States would be an enormous undertaking — arguably the most complex measurement transition in history. Here's a comprehensive breakdown of why it would be so difficult, what it would cost, and how it's been tried before:

---

## 🌍 The US Is (Almost) Alone in the World

There are over 195 countries in the world, and all but three of them use the metric system. Those three — Liberia, Myanmar, and the United States — continue to use variations of the imperial system. Still, America is the only industrialized nation in the world that does not conduct business in metric weights and measures.

---

## 📜 It's Been Tried Many Times

The US catches a lot of grief for never switching to the metric system, but the fact is, it tried several times.

- In 1790, Thomas Jefferson put forth a proposal for a decimal-based national measurement system that would bring uniformity in currency, weights, and measures across the country. It failed.
- In 1968, a study was approved by Congress which recommended a national conversion to metric units. Again the movement was stymied by lack of popular support — a Gallup poll showed that 45 percent of Americans were opposed to the switch.
- A significant push took place in the 1970s. On December 23, 1975, President Gerald Ford signed the Metric Conversion Act into law, creating a board tasked with overseeing America's conversion to the metric system.
- However, its implementation was incredibly slow and then virtually immobile, as no one willingly wanted to change to the metric.
- U.S. customary units have been defined in terms of metric units since the 19th century, and according to United States law, the SI has been the "preferred system of weights and measures for United States trade and commerce" since 1975. The U.S. even has a national policy to adopt the metric system. Under Executive Order 12770, signed in 1991 by President George H.W. Bush, all U.S. agencies were required to adopt the metric system. However, conversion was made not mandatory, so U.S. customary units remain in common use.

---

## 🏭 The Core Challenges

### 1. **Cultural Inertia**
There are real reasons for not switching that have nothing to do with American exceptionalism. For one, there's just cultural inertia — imagine what it would be like if all the numbers you used to measure your life suddenly changed.

### 2. **Industrial Infrastructure**
When the Industrial Revolution began in the country, expensive manufacturing plants became a main source of American jobs and consumer products. Because the Imperial System was in place at this time, the machinery used in these factories was developed to size in Imperial units; all of the workers were trained to deal with those units; and many products were made to feature them.

### 3. **Sheer Scale**
When the rest of the world switched to metric, it was mostly before or at the very beginning of the industrial revolution. Today, with mass production of goods, switching everything over to a new measurement system would be a gigantic undertaking. The US switching to metric this late in the game would be by far the largest, most complex transition of measurement systems in human history.

### 4. **Political Opposition**
Whenever the discussion of switching unit systems arose in Congress, the passage of a bill favoring the metric system was thwarted by big businesses and American citizens who didn't want to go through the time-consuming and expensive hassle of changing the country's entire infrastructure. Metric supporters argued that road signs were a crucial step in helping Americans get over psychological blocks to switching measurement systems. But Republican Charles Grassley killed proposed federal regulations that would have forced states to put up signs in kilometers, declaring "Forcing the American people to convert to the metric system goes against our democratic principles."

---

## 💰 The Cost

In 2015, NASA estimated a total conversion to the metric system would cost them $370 million. That sounds bad — but sixteen years earlier, they lost $125 million when the Mars Climate Orbiter crashed due to a confusion over units.

Students required to learn two measurement systems are more likely to be confused, and the additional time spent teaching both systems has its own implied cost. One researcher estimated that a full conversion to a single measurement system would save roughly 71 days in the classroom, and that metric calculations can generally be completed 45% faster — with full conversion saving an estimated $17.6 billion in education alone.

---

## ⏱️ How Long Would It Take?

Looking at other countries as a guide:
- The fastest approach — a "Big Bang" method — involves simultaneously outlawing pre-metric measurement, converting all government publications, and changing education to metric. India used this method, and its changeover lasted from April 1960, when metric became legal, to April 1962, when all other systems were banned.
- The UK and Canada used a slower phase-in method, and the process is still not complete in those countries. Japan also took a long time — about 70 years — with this method.
- The metrication process can take years to implement and complete: for instance, Guyana adopted the metric system in 2002 and was only able to make it mandatory in local trade in 2017, after the metric system was fully adopted in schools.

---

## ✅ The US Is Already Partly Metric

It's worth noting that the US is not entirely metric-free. Coke bottles are sold in liters, so is wine, medicine is measured in milligrams, food nutrition labels are metric, and athletic events like the 100-meter sprint or 5K race are fully metric.

---

## 🔑 Bottom Line

A full switch would be **extremely difficult** — requiring massive infrastructure changes, re-education of the entire population, overhaul of road signs, manufacturing retooling, and sustained political will across decades. It's not impossible (many large nations have done it), but the US's unique size, entrenched industrial base, and strong cultural resistance make it one of the most daunting public policy challenges imaginable. Most experts agree the benefits (global standardization, reduced errors, educational savings) would outweigh the costs — but getting there would be a monumental effort.
